s: The unnamed woman silently prepared for the great change while continuing to care for others. She finally lay down and fell asleep peacefully, being gathered into the Everlasting Arms.

The land from which the speaker's mother came is described as lying along an amber Adirondack river flowing to blue Ontario, with rock-maples, wheat fields, and bitter northern winters. The mother came from this land to college, where she questioned the future years and learned under the light of her lamp. Science became her bridegroom, and together they loved and learned. The mother's husband found and gave her the moons of Mars.

The land from which the mother came has an amber Adirondack river flowing through hills to blue Ontario. Staunch rock-maples grow along its banks, wheat fields lie beneath drifted snow, and the summer sun disappears into the lake.
The mother came from the northern land to college, questioning the future years. Her lamp of knowledge burned through the bitter winter gloom, and she loved and learned with Science.
Science is portrayed as the bride whom the mother's husband wed. Science and the mother's husband together loved and learned.
The mother's husband is portrayed as Science's groom. Like Orion hunting down the stars, he found and gave the mother the moons of Mars.
Mars is associated with moons that the mother's husband found and gave to the mother.
The moons of Mars were found by the mother's husband and given to the mother.

The document is a novel of Rudolph Hackh’s arrival in a Chinese treaty-port community and his transformation during plague, political unrest, and siege. Bound for a new post with Fliegelman and Sons, Rudolph is initially preoccupied with his attraction to the married Mrs. Forrester. Sent to replace Zimmerman at Stink-Chau, he is welcomed by Maurice Heywood into an isolated European circle that includes Doctor Chantel, Otto Wutzler, Miss Drake, Captain Kneebone, the Forresters, and the Reverend James Earle. A plague, signaled by disturbed rats and followed by deaths, introduces the community’s vulnerability. As Rudolph settles into a former Portuguese nunnery, learns Chinese, and encounters local poverty, religious conflict, and hostility toward foreigners, his outlook begins to change. He rescues an abandoned infant, sees the overcrowded hospital run by Miss Drake, and witnesses persecution of Christian converts, especially Chok Chung. Tensions mount around Fang, the Sword-Pen, who is connected to the secret White Lotus lodge. Heywood infiltrates the lodge and learns that its members are preparing an uprising, though he cannot discover its exact date. Meanwhile, Rudolph’s romantic fixation and a planned duel with Chantel are overtaken by the larger crisis. The foreign residents fortify the nunnery as warnings, anti-foreign placards, stolen gun parts, and attacks multiply. During a celebratory dinner, the uprising begins with the cry of “Kau fai.” Rudolph risks himself amid fires and fighting, then rejoins the defenders after witnessing the threatened torture of a Christian captive. The nunnery endures a prolonged siege: attackers use rifles, arrows, ladders, a stink-pot, and underground mines. Kempner dies saving the defenders, while Rudolph and Heywood discover and destroy the enemy’s powder preparations. With ammunition dwindling and Wutzler apparently dead, the women and survivors escape by a Hakka boat. Heywood remains behind after attacking Fang near Wutzler’s displayed body and is presumed killed. Captain Kneebone guides the fugitives downriver; Mrs. Wu, the Pretty Lily, repels an attacking craft. At sea, Rudolph and Miss Drake reflect on Heywood’s influence, until Heywood unexpectedly returns alive in a fishing boat, bringing the survivors’ journey to a joyful close.

Rudolph Hackh is a young German, a Baltic native who had lived in Bremen and worked as a clerk at twenty-one before becoming a shipping agent in China for Fliegelman and Sons. On his first journey to the Far East, aboard a German mail-boat and bound for China, he is homesick, timid, and romantically absorbed in Mrs. Forrester; he is crushed to learn she is married. He arrives at Stink-Chau to replace Zimmerman as manager, a new foreign station employee facing an unfamiliar Chinese city, plague fears, and chaotic office accounts. Friendship with Maurice Heywood draws him into local social life, while Dr. Earle's chapel address changes his perception of Chinese townspeople as human beings rather than devils or images. He survives the pestilence, studies Chinese, and settles into a former Portuguese nunnery assigned to him. His impulsiveness and emerging conscience appear when he rescues an abandoned infant girl from an island, takes her to the hospital, and promises funds for the child. His attachment to Mrs. Forrester and anger at Dr. Chantel lead him into a duel despite being a novice who knows nothing of swords; practice leaves his arm wounded, and Heywood substitutes for him. Later, called the "spare man," Rudolph escorts Mrs. Forrester home, protects her from a buffalo, and is pleased to be recognized as brave and honest. The records end with his return home to find most of the Mausers disabled by missing side-bolts.

Mrs. Forrester is a married Englishwoman who identifies herself as more French than English, wife of Gilbert Forrester, and an actress. Traveling alone in second class directly to Hongkong, she befriends Rudolph and encourages his conversation and romantic excitement, though he learns she is married when the ship’s doctor uses her title. She is distressed by Monsieur Jolivet’s death, rushes sobbing into the club for help, collapses into the protection of the dark-eyed girl, and remains shaken as singing resumes. Later, at a tiffin gathering at an ancient pagoda, she is lively and central to the audience: she tells stories, plays the Chinese lute, and sings several songs. She invites Rudolph up the tower, says she has thought of him, and touches his arm sympathetically before Maurice Heywood interrupts. On a morning ride with Rudolph, she challenges him to learn what is on the island and laughs at his pony in the mud. But when he returns with an abandoned infant girl, the child’s filth and suffering shock and disgust her. Saying she cannot bear suffering, she refuses to enter the hospital and leaves before Rudolph emerges.

Captain Kneebone, a wealthy captain of the Tsuen-Chau and friend of Cesare Domenico, assumes command of a boat after Heywood is believed dead. He delays along the shore, watches for danger, and grieves intensely, sharing his sorrow with Miss Drake. The episode ends with his astonished awakening when Heywood returns.
is_a ship [bound for Shanghai and Japan ports] The Tsuen-Chau is a ship bound for Shanghai and Japan ports. Its captain observes the activity in Port Said with Cesare Domenico.

Port Said is a crowded, noisy meeting place at the Suez Canal, containing Bar la Poste and filled with ships, travelers, soldiers, laborers, and many nationalities. It unfolds as Rudolph moves through its streets, visits a German shipping-office, and boards a German mail-boat.
Rudolph travels along the Suez Canal after leaving Port Said. As the ship moves through the Canal and the Bitter Lakes, he watches the West disappear and thinks, "Good-by to the West!"
is_destination_of Mrs. Forrester [directly] Hongkong is Mrs. Forrester's destination, as Rudolph learns from her and from the tag on her deck-chair.

China is the distant destination of Rudolph Hackh’s appointment, imagined by him as mysterious, old, and difficult to understand. It first appears as a sullen, inhospitable coast approached by ship. It then unfolds through a desolate coast and muddy river, ruins, war-junks, boatmen, coolies, and a crowded native town near Stink-Chau, while European residents live separately at the settlement’s edge. An excursion reveals rice-wine fields, bamboos, river traffic, fishermen, and ruined forts, alongside hostility toward foreigners.
recalls Zimmerman The dispatch Rudolph receives after arriving orders, "Zimmerman recalled; take his station; proceed at once." It directs Rudolph to replace Zimmerman immediately.

l: Rudolph's appointment in China, Dragon's Blood
s: assigns Rudolph Hackh [to Zimmerman's station] Rudolph's appointment sends him to take Zimmerman's station in China. He receives the relevant dispatch after reaching the port and is ordered to proceed at once.

l: Rudolph's voyage to the Far East, Dragon's Blood
s: ends_at China Rudolph's voyage carries him from Port Said through the Suez Canal, the Red Sea, Aden, Colombo, Penang, and Singapore toward the Far East. The journey begins in homesickness and uncertainty but becomes intensely important to him because of Mrs. Forrester.

l: Rudolph and Mrs. Forrester's romance, Dragon's Blood
s: Rudolph and Mrs. Forrester develop a brief romantic intimacy during the voyage, sharing conversation and a deeply emotional moment on the deck. Rudolph's hopes collapse when he learns that she is Mrs. Forrester rather than an unmarried Miss Forrester.

denotes first-time visitor to the Far East Mrs. Forrester calls Rudolph a "griffin" because he is making his first visit to the Far East. She describes griffins as "nice little monsters" and teasingly characterizes Rudolph as a moral, inexperienced young traveler.

Heywood is a young English hunter and foreigner in China, living in Stink-Chau in a house with dogs, debt, limited arms, and a cynical, increasingly taciturn outlook. He first meets Rudolph Hackh while shooting by the river, brings him into the settlement, hosts him, and becomes his close friend, companion, protector, and eventually proxy. He introduces Rudolph to the club and local figures, recognizes the rats as warning of plague, investigates killings and agitation connected with Fang the Sword-Pen, and admits that the town's terror and the likelihood of dying there trouble him. His loyalty and practical courage become central. Outraged by Doctor Chantel's insult, he fears Rudolph's duel will be fatal because Rudolph cannot fence; after trying to prevent it, he fights Chantel in Rudolph's place and helps repel rioters. Warned by Wutzler of coming violence, he infiltrates the White Lotus lodge, witnesses its ritual, survives discovery and attack, and returns with evidence of danger. As attack approaches, Heywood presides over the council while deferring to older men, presses for the nunnery as a fortified refuge, refuses to abandon native converts, and organizes scaffolding, loopholes, arms, and defenses. He warns Miss Drake to leave, yet remains beside her. Captain Kneebone's lottery win brings Heywood half-shares and an invitation Home, but the Black Dog's assault interrupts those hopes. During the siege, Heywood commands from the pony-shed roof, conserves ammunition, welcomes Rudolph back into the compound, directs resistance, investigates the Hakka boat and enemy tunneling, enters the mine, captures a coolie, and arranges an explosion in the enemy powder. As supplies fail, he helps prepare the women's escape. Seeing Wutzler's displayed body, he attacks Fang and vanishes, apparently dead. He then returns alive after escaping the attackers, killing pursuers, and reaching the boat by fisherman. Wounded only by an arrow scratch, he rejoins the group, sits quietly with Miss Drake, and proposes that Rudolph go Home with them.

contains the club [a gathering place for European residents] Stink-Chau is a bleak, isolated settlement reached by river after a long journey from the coast. Its European residents live together on the edge of the native town without a concession or bund, and the settlement is threatened by the plague.

The river is a waterway flowing irresistibly downstream toward the sea, at once dark, placid, mysterious, and at times broad, golden, painfully bright, and almost solid beneath savage sunlight. It is a route, a boundary, and a field of danger. At first it offers people cut off by land a possible way to reach the nunnery, while cries and activity rise along its bank. It carries jars, a funeral barge, pursuing and hostile boats, drifting fishing-boats, smoke, and the Hakka boat; Chok Chung is shot in its shallows. Though it can seem peaceful and safe, its landing is watched by concealed Chinese forces. The Hakka boat exploits the opposite shore, a crossing above, and the ebb to escape into midstream. As evening changes the water from copper to iron-gray, the boat drifts downstream through the night, until the river gives way to the sea.
employs Rudolph Hackh [as agent] Fliegelman and Sons employ Rudolph Hackh as their agent at Stink-Chau. Their firm previously employed Zimmerman, whose replacement Rudolph becomes.

Gilly is a European resident of the Stink-Chau colony, described by Heywood as its only gentleman. Married to Mrs. Gilly and identified as Bertha Forrester’s husband, he is a club member who welcomes Rudolph and discusses plague preparations, including fumigation, while wishing his wife were not returning. After her journey, he says she is resting and, despite initial embarrassment, joins the club concert by singing a French song about Tonkin. He is also linked to the hunting operation as a speaker of obvious conclusions. During the siege, Gilly holds the water-gate post, learns that Bertha Forrester has departed by boat, returns armed with Kempner’s rifle and belt, and volunteers for the first difficult position, including hazardous underground work.

Wutzler is a nervous, shy, isolated European resident of Stink-Chau who lives in Wutzler's house. Described as a German-speaking coolie, a white man, and a German-Chinese hybrid in appearance and dress, he has a frail, black-haired body resembling a puny ape and a Chinese wife whom he regards as shameful. He owns a repaired but damaged mechanical laughing box and considers himself a coward, as does Herr Heywood. He first greets Rudolph at the club and withdraws to his paper, then warns that the rats' behavior is ominous. At home, dressed in Chinese clothing, he anxiously feeds Rudolph and Heywood, praises Heywood's loyalty, fears being forgotten amid plague and violence, and blesses them brokenly. During the attack, he revives Rudolph with rice-brandy, guides and hides him through smoke and fire, and reports that Rudolph's friends are trapped. He disguises himself in a dead musketeer's clothing, leads Rudolph onward, then fires to confuse pursuit. He writes a coded message on an arrow, and ultimately the hostile forces display his head and body after his death.
Ah Pat, a compradore and messenger for Heywood, reports that the tunnel is empty while sappers eat, then leads Heywood and Rudolph to a newly raised mound and shaft.

Chantel is a French-speaking French doctor, Julien’s brother, and a striking but bitter, mocking figure among the club’s white men. Early in the crisis of rats and plague, he speculates that an earthquake may explain the rats, supports fumigation with chloride of lime and charcoal, and notes bitterly that the danger does not attack Europeans because Julien remains alive. After attending Monsieur Jolivet, he is disinfected, announces Jolivet’s death from plague, forbids others to visit the dead man, and later sings with the group. Chantel’s conflict with Rudolph becomes central. Seen riding with a woman and later at the Flowery Pagoda, he immediately inspires Rudolph’s hatred. At the club he taunts Rudolph, heroes, and a lady; after Rudolph strikes him, he calmly arranges a duel. Known as a beautiful, highly skilled swordsman and expert fencer, he accepts Heywood as Rudolph’s substitute, dominates the encounter, and agrees to postpone it only after being struck in the face and breaking his sword. He continues to mock danger, defenses, converts, and the magistrate at the war board until Heywood silences him. Later, at dinner, Chantel appears melancholy and suspicious and slips away after Mrs. Forrester signals angrily. In the end, he struggles with Bertha and attempts to take her away by boat, offering a stocked escape vessel, carrying her belongings, pulling her aboard when Rudolph hesitates, and striking at Rudolph with a boatman’s pole.

l: European residents of Stink-Chau, Dragon's Blood
s: herd_together_at Stink-Chau [on the edge of the native town] The European residents live together in an isolated group on the edge of Stink-Chau, where they rely on liquor, the club, and one another for diversion. They gather at the club after the rats appear and discuss whether the event is an earthquake or a warning of plague.

are_a_sign_of the plague [early warning] Rats emerge in scores around Wutzler and move through the lantern light without fear of the people. They repeatedly spring upward with short, agonized leaps before disappearing into the darkness.

The plague is a pestilence and the immediate danger threatening Stink-Chau, present in the surrounding settlement and aboard the Fa-Hien. Its first notice comes with rats emerging and leaping strangely. It causes fear among the expatriate community, dominates Rudolph's fears, and fatally strikes Monsieur Jolivet; Dr. Chantel reports his sudden death and his own disinfection. Quarantine shapes shore activity, while Captain Kneebone keeps two afflicted coolies topside under the boats. In town, reports say people are dying in Silk-Weafer Street, and residents hang nets and thorns against plague-goblins, imagined as sheltering frightened women and children. After explanations involving weather, soldiers, a kite, a paper effigy, and geomantic forces, the pestilence disappears. Rudolph is relieved, while an uncounted number of dead join the host of ancestors.

warns_of the plague [according to the colonists] The rats' behavior is treated by Wutzler as a warning, or 'warnung.' The other Europeans recognize it as an ominous sign and begin considering measures such as chloride of lime, charcoal, and fumigation.

l: the rats' mass emergence and leaping, Dragon's Blood
s: occurs_at the club [outside the street door] The rats' mass emergence occurs outside the club at night, where they huddle and move through the lantern light. Their repeated upward leaps resemble drowning creatures struggling against an invisible flood, and their departure is likened to answering the summons of a Pied Piper.

The club is a social club in the settlement: a gloomy upper-story loft in Stink-Chau with billiard tables and little comfort, where European residents gather. It first serves as the setting for Rudolph’s introduction to Wutzler, Gilly, and Doctor Chantel, while rats appear outside. On Ladies’ Night it hosts foreign residents for billiards, piano, conversation, and singing, briefly sustaining normality before plague news interrupts. Later, oppressive heat and disorder dominate as men drink, play cards, and quarrel; Rudolph confronts Dr. Chantel there. Its poor facilities, improvised drinking vessels, dead cushions and billiard balls, and no veranda, underscore its decline.

Flounce is a small fox-terrier, affectionately called Foreign Dog by Miss Drake. On a voyage she first recognizes Heywood, barks at a hostile approaching boat and draws gunfire through the sail, then whimpers and joyfully leaps at Heywood when he returns aboard; he says she alone knew he was alive.

l: the Fa-Hien's arrival at Stink-Chau, Dragon's Blood
s: is_a arrival [of the Fa-Hien] The Fa-Hien, a sixteen-hundred-ton Scottish Oriental ship, leaves Rudolph overside near the coast after signaling for a sampan. Rudolph then travels by sampan up the river to Stink-Chau, where Heywood receives him.
Monsieur Jolivet, a Frenchman associated with the French school, goes there while ill with the plague and dies suddenly. He is a compatriot of Dr. Chantel.

Chinese townspeople are human city residents who speak Chinese. They fill rain-darkened streets, bazaars, shops, and alleys, carrying baskets, working, serving food, operating chairs, and conducting business around Rudolph. Their voices, clothing, signs, and customs make the city feel overwhelming and unfamiliar to him. By night they continue amid smells, noise, and labor; in the chapel they listen and question Dr. Earle, then react to a killing with hostile cries and defenses against feared plague-goblins.

Dr. Earle, identified as the Reverend James Earle, is a white-haired doctor, padre, and clergyman married to Mrs. Earle. An English-speaking expatriate at the club, he leads a Christian flock of native converts and serves at a nunnery; his hospital work is praised by the magistrate. Heywood calls him one of the district’s two most dangerous men. As danger threatens his flock and Chok Chung, Earle agonizes over whom to protect. During the siege, he recognizes a scroll message, helps Heywood decipher it with the Triad cipher, and learns that a Hakka boat waits across the river. He stays with a dying convert, buries him, and permits the others to leave.

Miss Drake is a young woman on a hospital and nunnery staff, a pupil at the nunnery, and a medical attendant devoted to the hospital and its children. Wearing plain white clothing, she receives an abandoned infant girl without surprise and takes her away for compassionate medical care. She works with Heywood and refuses to leave on the next ship despite danger, because she must remain faithful to a guiding dream that has changed: she once believed in a dark continent of lost souls, but now questions what they can accomplish there. At a celebration, she accepts Captain Kneebone's two-thousand-rupee gift for the hospital and children after initial hesitation. During danger she tends wounded men and prepares medicines, declining rest because she is too busy. Her love for Heywood becomes explicit as more than ordinary liking. In the final record, she shares grief with Kneebone, speaks to Rudolph of Heywood as a Happy Warrior, and expresses a belief that invulnerability means being greater than anything that happens to a person, while saying she had always sensed Heywood's return was possible.

Bertha Forrester is a woman and Gilly Forrester’s wife, known to the men at the club. Gilly financially supports her travels to Japan, Kashmir, Ceylon, and Home. She is initially shaped by Dr. Chantel’s account of Rudolph Hackh: she resents Rudolph’s escort and accuses him of being like other men. Once Rudolph explains the confrontation, she admires his courage and honesty, likes that he is brave and different, and suggests she could be a better friend. Before an alarm, Bertha panics at her house, ransacks her treasure and belongings to decide what to save, clings to Rudolph, and urges him to leave with her by boat. When he refuses, Chantel pulls her aboard. She leaves the nunnery by boat rather than go to the besieged nunnery; Rudolph reports this choice to Gilly. During the attack, she is out of her wits.

Nesbit is a Cockney clerk and Heywood’s second. At a dinner, he proposes and helps stage an accident to stop a duel. During a riot, he recovers early, fights attackers with bottles, leads the Europeans into the breach, and suffers a forehead cut. Later he jokes and boasts about his part.
Sturgeon, a battered convivialist, serves as a reluctant, sympathetic second in a duel, brings swords, tends Rudolph, and joins the riot response.

The Europeans are foreign, white expatriate residents who attend the club and ride through the Chinese countryside after passing the inland wall. In “Passage at Arms,” they watch Heywood and Doctor Chantel fence, are attacked by neighboring hamlet men, pursue the rioters, and return exhausted after driving them away. Later, Rudolph and Wutzler hide among oil-jars, cross a battle zone, and return to the defended compound. During the siege, the defenders hold the northeast corner and water gate through attack, repair, and guard duty.
contains Fliegelman and Sons Office [in its dark city maze] Canton is not named directly in this unit.

is_a Chinese city [dark, maze-like and densely populated] The city is presented as a dark, labyrinthine bazaar filled with rain, crowds, shops, suspended signs, strange smells, and narrow covered passages. Rudolph experiences it as bewildering, oppressive, and almost unreal.

l: Fliegelman and Sons Office, Dragon's Blood
s: is_located_in the city [behind a portal in the dark maze] The Fliegelman and Sons Office is located in a dark Chinese building beyond the city streets. It contains a shrine, clerks, a European desk, and Rudolph's cramped inner room, where he begins sorting Zimmerman’s disorderly accounts.

includes accounts [disordered, mistaken and falsified] The office work consists of sorting through confused papers, accounts, mistakes, and falsifications left by Zimmerman. Rudolph works intensely and finds that methodical progress temporarily relieves his fear and homesickness.

l: the untimely rain and cold, Dragon's Blood
s: falls_on Canton [cold and continuous] The rain falls heavily from morning onward, flooding the daylight, running along tiled roofs, and turning the roads into muddy channels. It accompanies Rudolph's journeys and continues to drum on the roof while he works, reinforcing the gloom of the setting.

Mrs. Wu, formerly the Pretty Lily, is a capable Chinese boatwoman who owns and captains a sampan with her husband. She ferries Heywood and Rudolph, bargains and jokes with them, and is Rudolph’s friend. By the end, she takes control of a hostile craft’s steering and commands it.

Captain Kneebone is a peppery but capable sea-captain and navigator, associated with the small steamer Kut Sing. Early on, he receives Maurice Heywood and Rudolph aboard her, where two Chinese coolies have plague; hoping to evade quarantine at Koprah, he supplies his visitors with food, drink, and Spanish wine and pins his hopes of returning Home on a lottery. He later wins the Derby Sweepstake Lottery and arrives from Saigon at the nunnery with abundant provisions, servants, and drink. Though retired and claiming to have no ship, he stays through the crisis, hosts a lavish banquet, gives two thousand rupees through Miss Drake to the hospital and kiddies, and gives Heywood half his fortune and a journey Home. During the attack, the little captain takes command of the fugitives and defenses, directs Rudolph to cover, fires on the advancing Chinese, and judges the enemy's likely moves. As ammunition dwindles, he warns that the countermine is not enough, signals the Hakka boat, helps the fugitives board it, and finally recognizes and praises its concealed approach and steersman.

The Sword-Pen is Fang, a scholar and strict Confucian known as a clever, notorious mischief-maker and one of the district’s two most dangerous men. Tall, stooping, and dressed in a long robe or bright robes, he could have become a mandarin but prefers to live as a country gentleman. He hates the Jesus religion and foreigners, and Dr. Earle fears he will use Chok Chung’s killing for his purposes. After a stabbing, he is seen leaving the edge of a hostile crowd, and Heywood suspects he stirred the crowd against him. Fang is said to have brought the suit against Chok Chung and is identified as head of the White Lotus lodge. Through a black shrine image, he asks when the foreign monsters will perish and how the lodge will learn the appointed hour and day. Later, while seated on a white pony near a bier, he is attacked by Heywood with a halberd and knocked down in one blow.

Chok Chung is an extremely honest, mild Christian convert and merchant who owns a Chinese merchant’s hemp. In town, Au-yoeng kills him in his shop, alarming Dr. Earle because Chok Chung is one of his converts. In another account of his persecution, he is tried and questioned for following the Lord Jesus; after affirming his faith, his teeth are beaten out and he is thrown into prison, wearing soaked prison rags. Later he swims desperately toward a house while an armed boat pursues him, crying, “I am Jesus Christ!” He is shot in the shallows, sinks, and dies.

The village is a pastoral, happy place near the town, hidden under great trees and favored of the Influences. Its market-place lies on the route through it. At evening it is peaceful, prosperous, and active, until an old man warns Miss Drake and Heywood against the evil-minded West Quarter.

The Portuguese nunnery is a desolate, lime-coated house and missionary institution, and the home Rudolph Hackh moves into. Its quiet courtyards, servants, sounds, and views give him work, reflection, and a feeling of nearly recovering a former life. As anti-foreign agitation grows, red placards appear at its gate, and it is judged the best defensive position: it has limited exposed sides, a courtyard well, open surrounding ground, and an alarm bell. Heywood proposes fortifying it and sheltering native converts there. The nunnery hosts a dinner and Captain Kneebone's banquet before coming under attack; its occupants are said able to hold it while women are removed. During the uprising, Rudolph sees it through smoke and flames and thinks it is burning, though Wutzler says the shooting continues. Across a narrow lane from Rudolph's go-down, it receives stores he had ordered moved. It then becomes the defenders' besieged compound, with guns in the first bedroom, defensive positions, a counter-mine, Kempner's grave, and a river-facing water gate. After days of intermittent attack, bombardment, and repeated assaults, its walls are heavily pitted, but the small company is mostly unharmed and evacuates by the water gate.

l: the dead man’s killing of Chok Chung, Dragon's Blood
s: The records describe the killing of Chok Chung in his Chinese merchant’s shop. Au-yoeng, drunk and carrying a knife, enters the shop and kills Chok Chung after poverty, theft and recovery of Fuh-kien hemp, neighborhood pressure, and his belief that Chok Chung and the Jesus religion caused his troubles. During the quarrel, a half-naked ruffian is also described as stabbing himself, collapsing outside, and prompting hostility toward the merchant.

l: the Derby Sweepstake Lottery, Dragon's Blood
s: awards Captain Kneebone’s fortune [first prize] Captain Kneebone says that he has won first prize in the Derby Sweepstake Lottery. He says the money is safely credited to him at the H.K. and S. in Calcutta.
is_destination_of Captain Kneebone [after retirement] Captain Kneebone announces that he is retired and going Home. He also says that he has come to take Maurice Heywood Home.

are_called Foreign Dog [as an insult by hostile Chinese] Heywood and Rudolph are foreign men traveling through a Chinese district during a plague scare. After the stabbing, the crowd reacts threateningly when Heywood is called a "Foreign Dog" and a "Jesus man," showing hostility toward the foreigners.

Dr. Earle, a missionary married to Mrs. Earle, preaches earnestly at the Jesus Religion Chapel, speaking directly to Chinese townspeople about their shared humanity. After learning from Heywood that Au-yoeng killed Chok Chung, he warns that Fang the Sword-Pen may exploit it for trouble.

Au-yoeng, an impoverished cormorant-fisher after his birds died and luck failed, nearly starved, stole Fuh-kien hemp, endured neighbors’ pressure, blamed a merchant and the Jesus religion, killed Chok Chung while drunk, and died by his own hand.

The white men in this unit are Rudolph and Heywood, who move through the Chinese town, attend the chapel, report Chok Chung’s killing to Dr. Earle, and visit Wutzler. Their presence and status make them targets of hostility and connect them to the tensions surrounding the Jesus religion.

Christian converts, cut loose from their people by foreigners, become strangers in their own land; despite discordant chapel singing, Heywood urges sheltering them at the nunnery and using them to defend it.

witnessed the dead man’s killing of Chok Chung [silently at first] The mob at the scene of Chok Chung’s killing initially stands dumb and acts as an audience. Its hindmost members then begin shouting insults such as “Foreign Dog” and “Goat Man” after the white men step outside.

is_a Christian chapel [in a narrow room between a butcher's shop and a book-shop] The Jesus Religion Chapel is a long, narrow room between a butcher’s shop and a book-shop, where Chinese converts and inquirers gather under Dr. Earle’s preaching. Rudolph and Heywood visit it to hear the service and discuss the killing of Chok Chung with Dr. Earle.

The Chinese town is a hostile, crowded maze of alleys, galleries, dark corridors, and quarters, including a Jesus Religion Chapel, a rival lodge building, the dangerous West Quarter, and a gate left dark and open at nightfall. By night it remains active with labor, commerce, noise, smells, dim lanterns, rumors of plague, fear of supernatural forces, and dangerous unrest among its dregs. Heywood and Wutzler pass through it and escape by an unlighted gate; later Miss Drake and Heywood avoid its unfriendly streets, skirt its walls through an outlying hamlet, and reach the open road.

Wutzler’s house is a small, clean, sparsely furnished home hidden behind a black lane and a toy courtyard. It contains Chinese decorations, a European lamp, a household that flutters anxiously around its guests, and Wutzler’s damaged mechanical laughing box.

The Jesus religion is a new faith preached by Dr. Earle, represented by his chapel and Chok Chung, an honest Christian merchant. Hostile placards link it to foreign missionaries and accuse it of confusing converts. Au-yoeng blames it for suffering, while Dr. Earle fears violence will inflame opposition.

l: Au-yoeng's theft of Fuh-kien hemp, Dragon's Blood
s: was_addressed_by the elders of Au-yoeng's neighborhood [the hemp was found and nearly all restored] When his cormorant birds died and he faced starvation, Au-yoeng stole about a hundred catties of Fuh-kien hemp. Chok Chung recovered nearly all of it through the elders of Au-yoeng’s neighborhood and let the matter drop, but the neighbors continued to persecute Au-yoeng.

l: the Christian chapel service, Dragon's Blood
s: The Christian chapel service includes discordant singing, Dr. Earle’s forceful sermon, and questioning by Chinese inquirers. The service affects Rudolph deeply, and even Heywood acknowledges that Dr. Earle delivers his message effectively.

l: Wutzler's mechanical laughing box, Dragon's Blood
s: Wutzler’s mechanical laughing box is a damaged music machine that Captain Kneepone gave him after it was worn out. Wutzler repairs it so that it plays one remaining song, a metallic American voice repeating manic laughter that unsettles Heywood.

Gilbert Forrester, a senior member of the settlement and one of the white men, is a dinner guest and defender of the nunnery. During the war board, he proposes defending his house but admits his plans are vague and yields leadership to Heywood. He later survives gunfire, refuses to leave the water gate, and finally boards the Hakka boat.

Kempner, a defender at the northeast corner with long, thin arms, doubts the position can hold amid uproar, catches and returns a burning stink-pot cylinder, is killed, and is buried quietly beside the pit near the former chapel.

hosts the tiffin at the pagoda Rudolph refuses to join the party for tiffin at the Flowery Pagoda while brooding over Chantel and the equestrian encounter. The text does not otherwise describe a visit to it in this unit.
The ancient pagoda, a ruinously overgrown lilac tower in a grove, hosts a tiffin gathering; from its upper rail Rudolph and Mrs. Forrester view the countryside until Heywood interrupts them.

l: the notice forbidding drowned girls, Dragon's Blood
s: A placard on a stake beside the pond states that girls may not be drowned there, transforming the beautiful scene for Rudolph into one with an older, darker, more implacable character.

includes Chantel [paired with a woman rider] Rudolph and Maurice Heywood see two riders sweep across their path at twilight: a man leaning across laughing and a woman calling, "You really do understand me, don't you?" Rudolph recognizes the woman's words and manner, feels a sudden rage and possessiveness, and concludes that he should be riding there.

l: the tiffin at the pagoda, Dragon's Blood
s: The tiffin at the ancient pagoda gathers Mrs. Forrester, Gilly Forrester, Chantel, Nesbit, Kempner, the padre, Miss Drake, Heywood, Mrs. Earle, Rudolph, and Chinese servants. Mrs. Forrester performs; Rudolph drinks, entertains, and wins Miss Drake’s admiration.

l: the landscape from the pagoda, Dragon's Blood
s: The landscape from the pagoda includes an eastern sapphire ocean, glowing ancient walls, fields, hillocks, bamboo, pink paths, and a merchant on a white pony. Its timeless continuity, accompanied by bells and frogs, oppresses Rudolph.

The Chinese countryside is a landscape of green young-paddy terraces, vivid pink footpaths and new graves, bamboo and ancient burial places. Riders cross it toward an ancient pagoda, amid changing light, frogs, river, and distant walls, where beauty, antiquity, and menace mingle.

An abandoned infant girl lies naked, weak, filthy, and near death on an island near a burial depression among other infants’ remains. Rudolph finds and rescues her, and Miss Drake takes her to the hospital.

l: the hospital and kiddies, Dragon's Blood
s: The hospital, more crowded and underfunded than ever, receives Rudolph’s rescued infant as Miss Drake and a native woman try to save her; a local leper accuses its workers of stealing children for magic medicine.
A muddy, quaggy mound in the river, visited briefly by natives, is reached by Rudolph swimming; there he finds a shallow depression holding abandoned infants’ remains and a living infant girl.

is_a social crisis [involving abandoned infants] The island reveals that infants are being abandoned and left to die, with several bodies gathered in a shallow depression and rice placed beside them. Mrs. Forrester says that such things happen every day, while the hospital struggles with overcrowding and insufficient funds.

l: Rudolph's rescue of the infant, Dragon's Blood
s: Rudolph rescues an abandoned infant from an island's muddy depression, carrying her through sludge and river, wrapping her in his jacket, bringing her to land, and taking her to the hospital for treatment.

Rudolph and Mrs. Forrester ride ponies together at dawn along the river path as the hot season begins; after she challenges him to investigate the island, Rudolph finds an abandoned infant and takes her to the hospital.

faces the war threat [with limited arms and a distant gunboat] The settlement is threatened by unrest and possible attack, while its defenders have limited weapons and no nearby gunboat. The magistrate indicates that he has no means or recourse to help it.

l: the quarrel between Rudolph and Dr. Chantel, Dragon's Blood
s: is_a personal conflict [caused by an insult concerning the lady] The quarrel begins when Dr. Chantel disparages the lady and continues when Rudolph strikes him. Chantel treats the incident as a matter to be settled formally, while Heywood regrets that the quarrel divides the few men at the club when trouble is approaching.

l: the duel between Rudolph and Dr. Chantel, Dragon's Blood
s: The planned sword duel follows Rudolph’s quarrel with Dr. Chantel and Rudolph’s strike. Chantel is expected to choose swords; Heywood calls it plain murder because Chantel is a remarkable swordsman and Rudolph admits no knowledge of swordsmanship, though Rudolph sees possible escape.

Political unrest grows among the natives, partly fueled by the active Sword-Pen. During a hot night, concern deepens as Yamen runners escort Chok Chung to answer for a cormorant-fisher’s death, while Heywood warns that another act of trouble is coming.

The heat is an oppressive condition affecting the night and the men. It intensifies Rudolph's agitation, makes the air stagnant, sour, and breathless, spreads bad temper through the club, and contributes to reckless loss of self-control.

A pair of bell-hilted swords, originally belonging to Chantel's father, is chosen for the duel between Rudolph and Dr. Chantel because Chantel may choose and excels at fencing. Chantel prefers swords through vanity and skill, while Rudolph cannot tell point from handle. Sturgeon brings the pair; Rudolph is cut in practice, and Chantel breaks one sword in the rubble, with no replacement nearby.

l: the neighboring hamlet men, Dragon's Blood
s: The neighboring hamlet men gather to watch foreigners fence, then riot by throwing cocoanuts, sticks, clay, and plaster before fleeing a European charge. Later, as rioters, they search Rudolph's go-down, seize and persecute a Christian captive for recantation, prepare the Lamp of Heaven, and flee after rifle fire kills or disables some.

is_a ruined European-house compound [used for the duel] The deserted garden contains the ruins of a European house burned by natives years earlier. Its high, ruined walls and breach provide the setting for the duel and the subsequent riot.

is_a sword fight [between Heywood and Doctor Chantel] The planned duel between Rudolph and Doctor Chantel becomes a bout between Heywood and Chantel after Rudolph is wounded in practice. Chantel appears likely to defeat Heywood, but the fight is interrupted by a riot, and it ends without a conclusion when Chantel's sword breaks.

l: the battle and disturbance, Dragon's Blood
s: A brief, violent attack by men from a neighboring hamlet begins when they hurl missiles at a duel. Europeans counterattack, disperse the rioters, and leave Nesbit and Rudolph wounded. The disturbance expands across the region, causing fires and attacks on houses and buildings. Amid crowds, weapons, shouts, smoke, gunfire, explosions, rockets, and alarms, Rudolph, Wutzler, Bertha, Chantel, and others struggle to escape or survive through fighting around several sites and a defended compound.

is_a imported goods [from a Hai-nan venture] Cocoanuts rain down on the duelists and spectators during the riot, striking Doctor Chantel in the face and hitting others in the group. The Europeans later lament the broken shells and empty baskets belonging to a vendor from Hai-nan.

Otto Wutzler is a German outcast and guide, related by marriage to Wutzler's wife's cousin. Disguised as a small coolie in a wicker hat and dirty blue clothes, with mangrove-bark coloring, he warns Heywood that riots are coming and explains the rivalry between the Triad and White Lotus. Knowing the White Lotus lodge-room's listening place, he leads Heywood there but refuses to stay. He later helps disguise another fugitive's escape, guides Heywood through alleys out of town, identifies the Black Dog as a cannon, and seeks to learn when it will fire.

The Triad is a secret band or society with protective signs and ritual. Its Heaven-and-Earth sign, including a marked leg, identifies members in the streets. Wutzler’s wife’s cousin is a Grass Sandal; members claim peaceful intent, though some oppose the White Lotus and admit Heywood through the first gate.

White Lotus is a secret band and brotherhood opposed to the Triad, thought extinct but reappearing under Fang the scholar. It meets at night in its lodge-room, where Fragrant Ones conduct initiations, swear recruits into brotherhood, drink blood, and plan bloodshed, an uprising, or massacre.
contains the bath-room [vaulted] Heywood's house is where he returns after escaping the town. He bathes, changes into a kimono, and finds Rudolph waiting in a white-washed room.

l: the White Lotus lodge-room, Dragon's Blood
s: is_a lodge-room [of the White Lotus] The White Lotus lodge-room is reached through a blind wall and a series of guarded chambers and concealed passages. Heywood enters it after passing three portals, but the unit ends before he sees the gathering above the crypt.

l: the Meeting of the Dragons, Dragon's Blood
s: is_a town gate [westward of Heywood's route] Heywood believes he must run westward toward the gate where dragons met. Wutzler ultimately leads him through an unlighted gate out of the town, but the text does not explicitly identify it by that name.

is_phosphorescent green-gold [boiling with luminous sea-fire at night] The travelers recognize that they have reached the ocean when the water becomes deeper and the boat gains buoyancy and sea-room. Phosphorus makes the ocean boil with green-gold witch-fire alongside the boat and turns its wake into golden vapor. The ocean also carries the fishing boat that brings Heywood back.

l: the White Lotus uprising, Dragon's Blood
s: is_planned_by White Lotus [with a date to be set] The White Lotus uprising is anticipated as part of riots that will place those marked for massacre in danger. Wutzler says the White Lotus will set the day for this violence during its meeting that night.

l: the case against Chok Chung, Dragon's Blood
s: The case against Chok Chung, a Christian merchant, is forced on the magistrate as a trap to test whether his padre will interfere; Chok Chung is questioned about following foreigners, beaten, and imprisoned.

l: the White Lotus initiation, Dragon's Blood
s: The White Lotus initiation is a nighttime ceremony for recruits. It begins with invocations and displays of sacred or symbolic objects, then recruits swear oaths beneath crossed swords, enforced by threats of death. A white cock is sacrificed, blood is mixed and drunk, recruits enter the army as brothers, and the day of planned violence is set.

l: the message from Otto Wutzler, Dragon's Blood
s: A serious coded message, signed O. W. and carried by arrow during a siege, directs defenders to light a fire at the water-gate steps to summon a waiting Hakka boat. Its later fragment urges them to listen, work quickly, use many bags, and keep watch.

l: the White Lotus passwords, Dragon's Blood
s: are_used_at the White Lotus lodge-room [to pass through three guarded portals] The White Lotus passwords consist of ritual questions and answers about the East, the Fusang cocks, the Red Flower Pavilion, Ten Thousand Thousand Pages, the deluge, the Eight Abbots, the Unicorn, and a peach tree. Heywood uses these responses to pass the lodge's three guards.

l: the White Lotus ritual, Dragon's Blood
s: The White Lotus ritual, said to ape Triad ritual, begins with a white-lime circle, right foot placement, and a declaration of unity; participants drink from a designated cup, may include blood drinking, answer symbolic questions, and are admitted through successive doors.

occupies the rival lodge building The rival lodge is active inside a higher building, where its members conduct a formal initiation and discuss the destruction of the foreign monsters. Its members pursue Heywood after he is discovered.
is_a brotherhood The Fragrant Ones receive new recruits into their army and brotherhood through an elaborate ceremony. They speak of the foreign monsters and await a signal involving the Black Dog.

The recruits are about a dozen novices of the brotherhood who enter the lodge disguised in coolie clothes, then undergo initiation by swearing to the Fragrant Ones and sharing blood offerings and a ritual drink.

l: the Master of Incense, Dragon's Blood
s: A ritual officiant in dove-gray silk and a scarlet turban, he conducts the White Lotus initiation by displaying objects, examining sponsors, reciting oaths, and pricking recruits over a goblet.

The Red Wand, ritual spokesman of the Fragrant Ones, ceremonially uses an abacus and tells Fang, the Sword-Pen, that the foreign monsters’ destruction is near; he begins announcing the day, but Heywood’s attack interrupts him.

l: the pursuing lodge members, Dragon's Blood
s: pursue Heywood [after his escape from the lodge] The pursuing lodge members follow Heywood after he is attacked, running through the streets and opening doors. Wutzler deceives them by sending another fugitive onward while Heywood turns into a dark alley.
Foreign missionaries are targeted for destruction by the Fragrant Ones, branded “Red-Bristled Ghosts” on hostile placards, and depicted as foreign monsters enemies wish to perish.

The Black Dog, or Hak Kau, is a nine-foot bronze cannon cast at Rotterdam in 1607 and used by the attacking Chinese forces. Identified first as a cannon whose bark is meant to signal the Fragrant Ones' action, it is reportedly seen in a shed in the town, then missing the next day while attackers await ammunition. During the attack, its heavy sound is recognized as having barked earlier than expected. In the assault it fires repeatedly from nearby, sending copper cash clinking along the wall; its report serves as a signal rather than battering the masonry with round-shot.

l: the rival lodge building, Dragon's Blood
s: contains the White Lotus initiation ritual The rival lodge building is a higher structure overlooking the long roof. Its shutter and chink allow Heywood to observe the lodge ceremony and nearly expose him to the people inside.

is_a escape [from the White Lotus lodge] Heywood escapes by sliding down the roof, seizing the attacking spear, and running through the streets. A stranger diverts the pursuers, and Wutzler guides Heywood through alleys and out of the town.
The white cock, a sacrificial animal in an initiation ritual, is seized and beheaded; its blood is caught in a goblet and mixed with the recruits' blood for the oath.
is_a weapon A lodge member throws a spear at Heywood through the shutter. The spearhead grazes Heywood's scalp and the shaft lands beneath him, allowing him to snatch it before fleeing.
is_a ritual object [used for ceremonial counting] The Red Wand rattles the brown abacus as a ceremonial act while the lodge awaits the answer concerning the day of its planned action.
contains blood [a mixture of human and cock blood] The goblet catches the white cock's blood and is filled from a brazen vessel. The recruits pass it from hand to hand, chant, and drink from it.
is_a celestial body The moon rises through the brown haze and begins to illuminate the roofs and tiles. Its approaching light increases Heywood's danger while he hides beside the shutter.

is_undetermined unknown [in the conversation about the Black Dog's signal] The signal day is not revealed. The Red Wand says that the hours are numbered and begins to announce the day, but the attack on Heywood interrupts him.

Rudolph is a young white man, a runner who brings urgent news from the river, a host and defender at the nunnery, and owner of his own go-down. He is Heywood’s longstanding friend and comrade, is associated with Miss Drake through shared grief and understanding, and has Bertha as a forsaken lover. Initially perplexed and comparatively raw, he is changed by danger, loss, and Heywood’s example into a more resilient man ready to defend others. At the nunnery, Rudolph receives the arriving party with awkward ceremony, helps make dinner a banquet, notices Mrs. Forrester’s angry signal, and is sent to find Chantel without alarming the women. Amid the uprising he runs to Bertha’s house, helps Chantel with Bertha, carries Bertha to the river, and refuses the boat so that he can return toward the fires and those left behind. Struck by Chantel’s pole, he is revived and aided by Wutzler. He follows Wutzler through smoke, reaches his go-down, hides from rioters, witnesses the Christian captive’s martyrdom, and, with Heywood’s help, escapes over a wall. Taking a rifle, he runs to the northeast corner to join the defense. There he obeys Captain Kneebone, fights at a loophole, learns Bertha has departed by boat, and finds the enemy digging beneath the defenses. Though initially resigned to this threat, he regains courage through Heywood, enters the mine tunnel, carries powder, restrains a coolie, and retreats before the explosion. During the escape preparations, Rudolph learns not to mistake one exploit for victory, helps oppose Gilbert Forrester, clears the stairs, and boards the Hakka boat. He mourns presumed-dead Heywood, warns of hostile boats, recognizes Mrs. Wu as the Pretty Lily, and anxiously watches pursuit at sea. Heywood’s return confirms the lesson of Rudolph’s ordeal: grief and experience have made him more seasoned, courageous, and seemingly invulnerable.

A local magistrate stationed at a neglected, dangerous post lacks means or recourse to defend the settlement. Reporting the war threat indirectly but honestly, he formally visits Heywood and privately warns that precious resources should not be wasted and the settlement must act quickly to protect itself.

is_a council The War Board considers whether the rumors indicate a real threat and discusses arms, ammunition, fortifications, coolies, and sand-bags. Heywood effectively takes command of the board's preparations.

Rudie's house stands by river and marsh, which protect two and a fraction sides; in the war board it is contrasted with the nunnery, the proposed fortified refuge considered more suitable for defense.
The war threat is still based on rumors, but Heywood believes the reports may mean business. The expected attackers are said to be waiting about ten days for more ammunition.

l: defense of the settlement, Dragon's Blood
s: Defense plans include stocking one house, fortifying it if necessary, lending coolies, building bamboo scaffolding, preparing sand-bags and loopholes, and raising a mound or platform. The nunnery is favored because of its position, water supply, surrounding terrain, and bell.

l: the proposed refuge at the nunnery, Dragon's Blood
s: The proposed refuge at the nunnery would shelter the native converts and possibly others cut off by land. Heywood supports it because the nunnery is less cramped, easier to defend, and reachable by river.

The settlement has one pair of good rifles, two revolvers, several shotguns regarded as weak weapons, twelve old Argentine Mausers, and three cases of cartridges. Heywood considers the ammunition limited and uncertain.

At the council meeting, the men debate the choice of a defensible house, the treatment of the native converts, available weapons, and preparations for a possible attack. The discussion is interrupted by the magistrate's visit and ends amid reports of disturbance near the river.

The Mausers are twelve old Argentine rifles, calibre .765, the settlement’s only real weapons. Left by Heywood’s predecessor with three cases of cartridges, they are kept oiled by Heywood, who considers them sound and takes them over for the settlement’s defense. They are first polished and orderly in a rack at Rudolph’s home, but Peng removes the side-bolts from all except two, crippling them. Six rifles are later recovered from the garden, mud, and shallow water. As an attack begins, the guns are located in the nunnery’s first bedroom.

borders the compound [with a little gate nearby] The pony-shed is defended by Heywood and serves as Rudolph's entry point back into the compound. Heywood lowers a rope from its roof so Rudolph can climb over the wall.
The nearest gunboat is described as being a long way away. Heywood says that the settlement is therefore quite helpless and cannot expect timely naval assistance.

A white-walled compound entered through a tiled gateway contains the nunnery; amid a siege, it shifts from first-night fighting and wreckage to quiet sleep among sand-bags and daytime fortification work under blazing sun.

l: the pursuit and shooting of Chok Chung, Dragon's Blood
s: is_a pursuit and shooting [of Chok Chung on the river] A boat crowded with yellow-bodied men and blue jackets pursues Chok Chung, firing a matchlock at him as he swims. The first shot misses, but a second shot strikes him when he reaches the shallows; the pursuers celebrate with yells and laughter while the onlookers argue about what the killing means.

Placards posted on both nunnery gate pillars and in the West Quarter warn of agitation. They promote anti-foreign action, accusing the “Red-Bristled Ghosts” of attacks on ancestral worship, mind-darkening pills, and taking babies’ eyes for silver. They call for missionaries’ expulsion, Tao-tais to assemble people, and patriots to join.

The anti-foreign agitation spreads around the town and nunnery, portraying foreign missionaries as religious and magical threats. Villagers warn Miss Drake and Heywood as placards recruit patriots to expel foreigners and advocate killing and burning.

is_a former ideal [of Miss Drake's work in the country] Miss Drake says that she must stand by her dream, both as it used to be and as it now is. She recalls that she once believed she understood the lovely and terrible world, its Maker and Master, and that she regarded the land as a dark continent of lost souls; she now looks back on those beliefs with wonder and regret.

attend the banquet [at the nunnery] The dinner guests enjoy Captain Kneebone's food, wine, announcements, and gifts, laughing and offering congratulations. When the attack begins, they listen to the disturbance as Heywood orders the shutters closed and directs everyone to their posts.
"Kau fai!" is shouted by voices below during the attack on the nunnery. The cry is repeated more faintly as the voices seem to move toward the sound.

A celebratory, lavish dinner replaces a planned meal when Captain Kneebone brings stores from Saigong. The banquet unfolds with abundant food, excellent wine, candles, conversation, and laughter, until an attack interrupts it.

is_hosted_by Captain Kneebone [as a celebratory banquet] The dinner begins at the nunnery before Captain Kneebone's provisions transform it into his banquet. Its celebration includes his announcement of his lottery winnings and gifts, but it ends abruptly when the attack starts.

is_deposited_at H.K. and S. [in Calcutta] Captain Kneebone says his fortune is greater than the old Kut Sing earned since its launching and that it initially frightened him and cost him sleep. He intends to distribute part of it while alive rather than wait to make a will after death.

belong_to Maurice Heywood [given by Captain Kneebone] Captain Kneebone gives Maurice Heywood half of his fortune, calling the arrangement half-shares. Heywood is stunned but accepts the offer after Miss Drake urges him not to spoil the captain's happiest evening.

l: the attack on the nunnery, Dragon's Blood
s: The attack on the nunnery is signaled by the Black Dog’s barking and approaches through darkness. Stones strike the open windows, followed by shouts, gongs, conches, and gunfire. Heywood orders shutters closed, directs the men to guns, and plans to hold the nunnery while evacuating the women.
is_at the nunnery [already erected] Heywood says that the scaffolding is already up and calls it fortunate when the attack begins. He appears to regard it as useful to the defense of the nunnery.

Native attackers are an armed, numerous group that first attack an uprising and move through darkness in crowds, fighting Rudolph amid burning houses while crying “Sha, sha.” They possess powder stored underground and shift from ineffective sniping to digging beneath the defenders, preparing an underground assault intended to blow up the defending position in one sweep.

During the attack, fires burn Heywood's house, the club, and Bertha's house, apparently reaching the nunnery or nearby buildings; flames, smoke, and sparks illuminate the region and conceal Rudolph and Wutzler.

The Hakka boat is a shallow-draft river boat with a bamboo-thatched roof, manned by boatmen and used for escape. It is stocked and ready to take fugitives down the river and along the coast; Bertha boards it, while Rudolph refuses and is left behind when Chantel orders it to shove off. Across the river, it waits as a signal craft, displaying a green flag and a rice-measure at its masthead, with a coded promise to come if a fire is lit at the water gate. Hidden among masts, it seems to vanish, then secretly works upstream, crosses above the fugitives, and drifts down beneath the river-wall to take them aboard. It carries them toward midstream and downstream toward the coast, passes a war-junk, reaches the roadstead, survives an attack by armed men after the Pretty Lily drives them away, and is later followed by Heywood's fishing boat.
The gunwale, polished by bare feet over many years, is a boundary between life and death: Rudolph leans on it as Bertha clings, then she refuses to cross and falls into mud.

A haggard, imprisoned Christian captive is seized in Rudolph's go-down, threatened with death and compelled to recant or die. Maintaining his faith, he chooses martyrdom, refuses demanded words, and is tortured with burning flour and oil until rifle fire interrupts.

are_a rebel soldiers [armed with muskets] The musketeers fire continuously from ragged earthworks while the disturbance continues. One wounded musketeer crawls away to die and is later used by Wutzler as the source of a disguise.
A go-down across from the nunnery holds disordered merchandise, shelters people briefly among bales and behind reeds, then rioters search and burn it.

The clay-pit is a place during the siege, connected by a mine tunnel to the surface. Rudolph first sees coolies working there; later he and Heywood hear digging and recognize the attackers’ underground danger. A shaft from the mound opens into its passage, enabling their descent, return with powder, and escape before the explosion.

is_a defensive position [on the nunnery wall] The northeast corner is heavily attacked but held by the defenders. Chinese forces reach its wall with ladders and scaling bamboos, yet the position remains secure after the stink-pot cylinder is thrown back.

l: the Lamp of Heaven, Dragon's Blood
s: The Lamp of Heaven is the rioters’ name for a punishment imposed on a Christian captive: they place a crown of flour and petroleum dough on his head and ignite it, leaving it smouldering when rifle fire interrupts them.

uses the Lamp of Heaven [as an instrument of execution] The Christian martyrdom consists of the captive's refusal to recant and his acceptance of death. Rudolph watches helplessly as the captive is crowned with burning dough, calls on the god across the sea, and is apparently rescued or at least spared by the sudden rifle volley.

Rudolph's transformation culminates when he returns to the compound after witnessing the Christian captive's ordeal. He feels freed from his former perplexities and admiration, takes up a rifle without needing a drink, and becomes ready to share his friends' clean and wholesome danger.

l: the attacking Chinese forces, Dragon's Blood
s: The attacking Chinese forces are a besieging force outside the nunnery, attacking from land, river, walls, fields, and underground. They use guns, arrows, copper cash, ladders, bamboos, a stink-pot cylinder, sniping, dummies, and attacks on both gates, while expecting reinforcements from up country. Their rush at the northeast corner is repelled when their cylinder explodes among them. They continue hiding around the nunnery, digging beneath its defenses, and storing powder near the clay-pit, but the powder is sabotaged and explodes. They later pursue Heywood but cannot stop the Hakka boat reaching midstream.

The water gate is a defensive position of the nunnery opening onto the river. During the siege, Gilly Forrester, converts, and others defend it against arrows and gunfire from the marsh; a fire signal is proposed but the route is judged covered. Later it is guarded, opened, and used for escape to the Hakka boat.

The high field's crest changes after the countermine is sprung and later becomes the site where Wutzler's body is displayed. Fang the Sword-Pen and his men are there when Heywood runs up the field and disappears over its crest.

contains Greek fire [in liquid form] The stink-pot cylinder is thrown onto the defenders' platform with a burning fuse. Kempner throws it back, and it bursts below the wall in jets of liquid flame that set clothing and powder-horns alight and scatter the attacking Chinese forces.

is_a code [used to decode the message] The Triad cipher enables Dr. Earle and Heywood to read the elaborate characters on the coded message. By separating and subtracting recurring character components, they recover the instructions concerning the Hakka boat and the water-gate signal.

l: the siege and assaults, Dragon's Blood
s: A prolonged, furious military encirclement targets the nunnery over nights and days, alternating pauses with outbreaks. Attackers use gunfire, river boats, battering-rams against both gates, dummies to draw fire, and eventually dig beneath the defenses. Defenders beat back the assaults but become exhausted and nearly out of ammunition as the threat escalates.

is_a attack [on the northeast corner] The Chinese assault begins with gunfire, arrows, and copper cash, followed by a rush of men carrying ladders, bamboos, and the stink-pot cylinder. The defenders repel it after Kempner throws the cylinder back, though the enemy resumes intermittent attacks afterward.

Kempner dies during the Chinese assault while defending the northeast corner, after throwing a burning stink-pot cylinder away from the defenders. His action helps end the assault; his weapon goes to Gilly Forrester and his body is buried at the nunnery.

l: the digging beneath the defenses, Dragon's Blood
s: A digging beneath the defenses is detected under the former chapel when Rudolph hears coolies in the clay-pit. Rudolph and Heywood listen, conclude attackers are digging, and the account ends before its purpose is revealed.

The coolies are manual workers assigned to mine-tunnel digging. Four are ordered into the sappers' tunnel, others assist Heywood and Rudolph at the shaft, and enemy coolies eat rice near clay-pit fires.

occupy the mine tunnel [during the excavation] The sappers have dug the underground tunnel and stocked it with powder, but they are absent when the defending party enters it. Their tunnel leads toward the clay-pit and the enemy's main powder supply.

A defending party occupies a nunnery under siege, resisting enemy mining and gunfire. As the enemy digs beneath them, Heywood and Rudolph enter the tunnel and sabotage its powder. After enduring heat, fighting, exhaustion, flies, and dwindling ammunition, the fugitives evacuate by Hakka boat while Heywood stays behind after attacking Fang.

contains the hospital room [within the defended compound] The courtyard provides a brief place of rest for Rudolph and Heywood, with wet flags, a candle, a well, and the sounds of water, bats, and occasional gunfire. They leave it when the compradore reports on the tunnel.

The mine tunnel is a damp, narrow underground passage through wet earth from the shaft toward the clay-pit. It contains a chamber with powder sacks and burden-carriers’ niches; Heywood and Rudolph use it to reach the enemy’s position amid danger.
contains the mine tunnel [at its outer end] The mine tunnel ends at the clay-pit, where enemy coolies sit around fires and eat rice. Its portal is protected by a bulkhead made from sacks of powder.
The powder supply is explosive material stored in sacks at the tunnel entrance as a supposed sandbag bulkhead. Identified as the enemy’s whole supply, it becomes Heywood’s target for sabotage.

The explosion follows a long delay after Heywood and Rudolph return to the surface. It strikes with the force of a mallet and sends a shower of clods over them, while Heywood concludes that the enemy has suffered a major setback.

The Hakka boat then approaches covertly, receives the women, converts, white men, and compradore, and carries them away while Heywood turns back to attack Fang.

s: A white body lies on a framework like a bier in the field, with a rough windlass nearby. Heywood recognizes the display as the hostile forces' treatment of Wutzler and reacts by attacking Fang.

s: is_a escape route [upstream crossing followed by descent with the ebb] The Hakka boat reaches the fugitives by working upstream along the opposite shore, crossing above them, and dropping down with the ebb along the shallow water beneath the river-wall. The fugitives board through the water gate and escape as the boat drifts into midstream.

resemble a dragon [in their long, finlike outline] The dragon hills appear as a dim range along the land, with sharper crests resembling the finny back of a leviathan. Rudolph compares their shape to a dragon and reflects that the mysterious empire beyond them continues its life despite his personal loss. Later, the hills fade from view while Rudolph watches the phosphorus and waits for signs of Heywood.

His return is revealed when he boards the Hakka boat alive, explaining that he escaped the attackers and reached a fisherman. The revelation brings astonishment and joy to Rudolph, Miss Drake, Captain Kneebone, and the other sleepers.

Captain Kneebone says that money is the only thing left between him and the grave, while Rudolph feels that his heart is vacant except for grief. Their grief becomes calmer when Rudolph and Miss Drake speak openly about Heywood and the qualities he taught them.

An Astronomer’s Wife, by Angelo Hall, is a biography of his mother, Chloe Angeline Stickney Hall, written for his daughter Peggy and the public. It follows Angeline from her impoverished childhood in Rodman, Jefferson County, through education, marriage, motherhood, reform commitments, and death. Her ancestry is traced through the Cook and Stickney families; her father, Theophilus Stickney, abandoned the family when she was young and died in 1842, leaving her mother and daughters in hardship. Angeline endured domestic labor, illness, and poverty but pursued study at Rodman Union Seminary, became a teacher, and developed interests in science, history, writing, religion, abolition, and women’s rights. Determined to attend college, she earned money through teaching, painting, and making tissue-paper flowers before studying at McGrawville and New York Central College. There she excelled, taught mathematics, embraced abolition, woman suffrage, and the bloomer costume, wrote prose and poetry, and graduated with an A.B. despite financial strain and illness. The book then introduces Asaph Hall 3rd, a former carpenter with self-developed mathematical ability, who met Angeline at McGrawville. Their affectionate courtship led to marriage in April 1856. The couple lived in Ann Arbor, taught at Shalersville Institute in Ohio, and moved to Cambridge in 1857 so Asaph could pursue astronomy. Angeline sustained their household, taught him German, encouraged his work, and participated in intellectual and political life, although their marriage included disputes about suffrage, poetry, wages, and dress. During the Civil War, they moved to Washington, where Asaph joined the U.S. Naval Observatory, observed Mars, and rose to a professorship; Angeline managed the family, aided friends and relatives, and supported his career. At their Georgetown home, Angeline raised Asaph, Sam, Angelo, and Percival with discipline, education, gardening, and moral care; all four sons graduated from Harvard College. She continued studying history, philosophy, genealogy, poetry, science, and religion, gradually moving from her mother’s theology toward Unitarianism and a faith reconciled with scientific inquiry. She encouraged Asaph’s search for the satellites of Mars. After recurring illness and lifelong labor, she died of apoplexy at North Andover on July 3, 1892. Later letters, a tribute by Augusta Larned, and an epilogue portray her charity, intellectual vigor, domestic devotion, spiritual generosity, and enduring union with science and Asaph’s astronomical achievements.
