l: An Astronomer’s Wife, An Astronomer's Wife
s: A book by Angelo Hall, it biographies his mother Angeline Hall, telling her true typical American story while vindicating women’s education and offering lessons on marriage and financial security.

Angelo Hall, son of Angeline Hall, was born on September 16, 1868, at 18 Gay Street, the third child. Described first as fat and rosy, then healthy, bright, handsome, and active, he helped with household and garden work before becoming a college student in 1887. In 1908, at Annapolis, he wrote An Astronomer’s Wife, a biography of his mother addressed to his daughter Peggy and the public.

is_a granddaughter [of Angeline Hall] Peggy is Angelo Hall’s daughter and the immediate addressee of the biography. Her grandmother, Angeline Hall, died before Peggy was born, so Angelo writes to give Peggy a picture of her life.

Angeline Hall, born Chloe Angeline Stickney, was a college-educated woman, teacher, writer, homemaker, mother, and the wife of Asaph Hall. Described as a pioneer among college women, she believed women had the same capacities as men for knowledge, virtue, and truth, supported co-education, and pursued intellectual work through science, philosophy, history, genealogy, poetry, essays, and a planned teaching work on Prometheus. In her college days she wore the bloomer costume and enthusiastically supported abolition of skirts, though she and her husband later quarreled over woman suffrage, poetry, and the value of her work. Her life unfolded through strenuous service to family and others. At Shalersville Institute she taught, learned oil painting from Mary Gilman, and nursed Asaph Hall during a severe fever. During difficult years, including the war, she supported him materially and emotionally, cared for the family, joined him in Washington despite dangers and disease, and successfully advocated for his appointment to the vacant Observatory professorship; she later advocated for George W. Hill. She managed household and family affairs so that her husband could work, while doing cooking, washing, sewing, ironing, cleaning, and other work, commonly with one servant. At 18 Gay Street, where she lived for twenty-five years, she raised four sons, Samuel, Angelo, Percival, and Asaph Hall Jr., and sent them all through Harvard College. She taught them before academic age, demanded truth and obedience, organized their household and yard work, nursed them herself, and trained them in moral principles. Her domestic life also included gardening, concern for poor relatives, care for her mother and sisters, and leadership of the Stickney family after her mother’s death in 1878. Religious faith remained important: she was brought up in her mother’s church, became Unitarian, later withdrew after a church quarrel, and expressed a faith that had outgrown superstition in “To Science.” Late in life she participated in historical and philosophical societies, attended Academy meetings, performed charity work among poor people in Washington and Georgetown, and visited the Home for Destitute Women and Children for her last fourteen years. In declining health, bent from years of toil, she continued to travel, write letters, and visit the Adirondacks. She died of a stroke of apoplexy in her sixty-second year at North Andover, Mass., at Mrs. Berrien’s house.

Chloe Angeline Stickney, later Angeline Hall, was the sixth child of Theophilus Stickney and Electa Cook, born on All Saints’ Day in 1830 in Rodman. Fatherless from birth, she grew up solemn, industrious, and devoted to learning, beginning school at three, working from childhood, and developing ambitions for education and public distinction. She studied at Rodman Union Seminary and, from 1848, spent nine years alternating between teaching and being a pupil. An excellent, patient, firm teacher, she taught in several places, won her pupils’ respect and affection, and seldom used punishment. Poverty, poor health, and religious scruples complicated her determination to attend college. She raised funds through teaching painting and tissue-paper flowers, entered New York Central College, studied mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, Greek, German, and political economy, taught mathematics while enrolled, and graduated with an A.B. in 1855 despite an exhaustion-related breakdown shortly before graduation. At college she embraced woman suffrage and wore the bloomer costume; she also wrote poetry and maintained intense religious commitments. A sincere Baptist from age sixteen, she corresponded with Asaph Hall during their courtship, disclosed her father’s history before their engagement, encouraged his religious preparation, and married him in April 1856. Though often delicate or ill, she supported his scientific career through severe economy, teaching him German, encouraging his studies, and assisting his observatory work. Her religious views broadened, while she continued to seek truth, study nature, and reconcile science with religion. As wife, mother, and bread-giver, she made a home characterized by unselfishness, charity, justice, hospitality, and tender care, raising four sons. She welcomed poor and despised people without condescension, resisted false social distinctions, and avoided causing pain through wit. Her life ended after a silent decline; she died quietly, painlessly, and without complaint.

l: the American pioneers, An Astronomer's Wife
s: The American pioneers, an ill-fed, ill-clothed but forceful race, travel westward through wilderness seeking permanent homes, exemplified by Elisha Cook and his family.

Elisha Cook was a pioneer of the Black River Country who left Ellington, Connecticut, with his wife Huldah and children in January 1806. Father of Electa and grandfather to the Stickney girls, he became a kindly protector of the Stickney household and died in summer 1841.

Electa Cook, daughter of Elisha Cook and Huldah Pratt, married Theophilus Stickney in 1816 and became mother of Angeline, Chloe, and other Stickney girls. After Theophilus’s death, she married Milton Woodward and brought her unmarried daughters into his household.

Moses Stickney was a Revolutionary soldier, crack shot, husband of Mary Hastings, father of Mary Stickney, and paternal grandfather of Angeline Hall. Living in Jaffrey beside Mount Monadnock, he reportedly carried his musket at Bunker Hill and yoked oxen on his hundredth birthday.

Theophilus Stickney, Moses Stickney’s son, was a skilled carpenter and Electa Cook’s husband. After unpaid building work cost him his home and farm, he moved his family, returned to the Black River Country, became a drunkard, and left before Chloe Angeline was three. Absent from his daughters’ lives, he died in Rochester hospital on February 14, 1842, leaving them doubly orphaned.

contains Ellington [town in Tolland County] Connecticut was the New England home of Elisha Cook and his family before they began their westward journey in 1806. The Cook family left Ellington and Tolland County in search of a new home beyond New England.

l: Black River Country, An Astronomer's Wife
s: is_a wilderness settlement [destination of the Cook family] The Black River Country was the destination where Elisha Cook sought a home after leaving Connecticut. It was also the place where Theophilus Stickney returned after financial difficulties and where Chloe Angeline Stickney was born.

Rodman is a town in Jefferson County, with productive surrounding soil, abundant grain, and early distilleries. It is where Chloe Angeline Stickney was born, educated, and later taught in Heath Hollow. Its Cook and Stickney homes, district and singing schools, and Rodman Union Seminary shaped her early life and patient teaching.

l: the American Revolution, An Astronomer's Wife
s: is_a war [ancestor-defining conflict] The American Revolution is part of Angeline Hall’s family heritage through Moses Stickney, who served as a Revolutionary soldier. The narrative also recalls Burgoyne’s surrender, Fort Stanwix, Bunker Hill, Arnold, Morgan, and Washington’s army.

l: the Civil War, An Astronomer's Wife
s: The Civil War, anticipated by the Halls amid heated Boston meetings and fears of friends lost in battle, depleted the U.S. Naval Observatory staff, brought battles and wounded soldiers to Washington, and exposed Hall’s family to disease, danger, and hardship. It ended with army reviews through the city.

l: women’s higher education, An Astronomer's Wife
s: Women’s higher education is presented as a pursuit of knowledge and virtue for women as well as men, grounded in women’s equal senses, consciousness, perception, and intellectual capacities. Angeline Hall, a pioneer college woman, vindicates it by earning a Bachelor of Arts while sustaining family life and sending her four sons through Harvard College.
Intemperance is a destructive sin in Theophilus Stickney after his return to the Black River Country, causing Angeline Hall’s weakened nervous system and consequences extending to later generations.

l: the pioneer experience, An Astronomer's Wife
s: includes westward migration [with family and household goods] The pioneer experience is shown through difficult westward travel, settlement in wilderness, hard physical labor, and the effort to establish homes and farms. The pioneers are also portrayed as people who carried religious, cultural, and family traditions into new regions while facing financial and personal hardships.
Charlotte Ingalls, formerly Charlotte Stickney, was Angeline’s sister who married Edwin Ingalls, lived in Wilna, and became a capable, thrifty tavern hostess by 1842.

Ruth is Angeline Stickney’s sister and a briefly enrolled student at New York Central College. She joins Angeline’s plan for college at McGrawville, where they live on one dollar a week, have daguerreotypes taken in January 1852, and Ruth later attends college for short periods, including two months in 1854. Poor health forces her home and ends further study, but she financially supports Angeline and brings her home after Angeline breaks down before graduation. Ruth preserves a poem from memory, feels deeply lonely without Angeline, and later endures recurrent paralysis that threatens her husband Asaph’s prospects.
Milton Woodward, a strong-willed widower with ten children, marries Electa Cook, resists her daughters joining his household, supports abolition, and sometimes abuses Electa violently.

l: the Woodward family, An Astronomer's Wife
s: is_a family [of ten strong-willed children] The Woodward family included Milton Woodward’s five sons and five daughters. The children were described as strong-willed and often wrangling, while some ridiculed Angeline by calling her “Lady Angeline.”

l: the Stickney girls, An Astronomer's Wife
s: The Stickney girls became doubly orphaned after the deaths of their father, Theophilus Stickney, and their protector, Elisha Cook. With no brothers or father, the mother and four young daughters relied on their own resources and on one another.
Abolitionists were particularly prominent at New York Central College, which was described as a stronghold of abolition and counted John Pierpont, Gerrit Smith, and Horace Greeley among its patrons.

are_held_in bondage [under slavery] Slaves are described in Angeline’s composition as people held in bondage, half clothed and half starved, forced to labor under threat of whipping and sometimes driven away from their homes in chains. Angeline expressed pity for them and argued that freedom was as dear to slaves as to their masters.
Wilna was the town where Angeline went to live with her sister Charlotte after Electa Cook’s remarriage. Charlotte and Edwin Ingalls kept tavern there in December 1842, and Edwin taught Angeline.

l: Rodman Union Seminary, An Astronomer's Wife
s: The Rodman Union Seminary provided Angeline with three terms of schooling beginning in the fall of 1847. Her cousin Harriette Downs paid her tuition, while Angeline worked for her board and walked to school, even through deep snow.

l: the Woodward household, An Astronomer's Wife
s: Woodward household, a large difficult home at Dry Hill, employs Chloe Angeline Stickney as chief assistant and houseworker; for four years she performs extensive domestic labor while attending school.

l: Electa Cook’s second marriage, An Astronomer's Wife
s: Electa Cook’s second marriage, a church-arranged union with Milton Woodward, ended her independence and brought her daughters into a troubled household with Milton’s ten children.

Angeline’s education began in district school at age three, continued with Edwin Ingalls and Rodman Union Seminary, and included favored history, natural philosophy, grammar, arithmetic, spelling, singing, and composition despite work and difficult travel.

l: Angeline’s work in the Woodward household, An Astronomer's Wife
s: includes housework [baking, mopping floors, and milking cows] Angeline worked industriously at the Woodward farm from age twelve until 1847. She baked for the large family, mopped floors, milked cows through the snow, and at times performed most of the housework while helping her mother.
At fourteen, Angeline wrote compositions on the sugar maple’s uses and against slavery, winning George Waldo’s praise and encouragement to continue writing.

Slavery is presented in Angeline’s 1845 composition as an unjust robbery and piracy that deprives people of liberty, condemned by the Bible and maintained in the United States. Angeline argues that slaves value freedom, hopes the country renounces slavery, and later urges dissolving the Union rather than obeying the fugitive slave law to strike it a death blow.

Education is portrayed as a contested path from childhood schooling to college. Angeline’s early education includes district school, Edwin Ingalls, singing school, and Rodman Union Seminary, amid harsh school discipline. Despite financial hardship and opposition to women’s ambitions, she advances through teaching and study at New York Central College, where admission disregards race or sex but poor students work for food and lodging; Ruth leaves because of poor health. Asaph Hall 3rd begins serious study late, excels in geometry and algebra, and gains encouragement. The text criticizes conventional educational theory and treats college attendance as education’s intended continuation.

Christianity is presented as a source of divine enthusiasm for advancing knowledge, supported by arguments, symbolized by mountains, and considered a desirable condition shared by marriage. It begins in intense faith centered on prayer meetings, the Savior’s blessing, salvation, cleansing, and the Lamb’s Book of Life. It then emphasizes tolerance: human, theistic, moral, Christian, and Protestant identities outrank denominational division in marriage. Faith broadens beyond superstition and narrow theology through Unitarianism and searching in philosophy, history, and science, ending in a broad religious outlook that finds no necessary conflict between religion and nature study.

McGrawville is a college location offering education through an advertised manual-labor system. It enabled students to live cheaply while studying: Angeline Stickney began her college course there, arrived with Ruth in April 1852 so they could attend together, and later returned for her junior year. Asaph Hall 3rd came in 1854 to earn a living while studying and quickly solved a problem that had baffled students and teachers.

The district school in Heath Hollow, near Rodman, was where Angeline Stickney began teaching in 1848. She generally avoided punishment but used it decisively when necessary, and her pupils respected and obeyed her.

l: college course at McGrawville, An Astronomer's Wife
s: After beginning her college course at McGrawville, Angeline Stickney continued teaching while trying to study. A letter from this period shows that she had little opportunity for formal instruction and feared she would make limited progress.

Teaching occupied Angeline Stickney during much of the nine years before her marriage. She taught district schools, tutored in the family of Elder Bright, boarded around the district, and earned the affection of pupils through careful explanations, patience, gentleness, and resolute discipline.

l: marriage of Angeline Stickney and Asaph Hall, An Astronomer's Wife
s: The marriage of Angeline Stickney and Asaph Hall began on a Monday morning in early April 1856, after Hall visited her family and joined her in Wisconsin. They traveled to Ann Arbor and settled there while Hall studied astronomy and French. Though they faced poverty, Angeline’s frail health, illness, and Hall’s severe fever, the marriage was fortunate, marked by happiness, mutual care, encouragement, and support.

l: New York Central College, An Astronomer's Wife
s: New York Central College, also called Central College, is a college at McGrawville in Cortland County and a forerunner of Cornell University. An unpopular institution in the surrounding world, it is a stronghold of reformers and abolitionists, supported by John Pierpont, Gerrit Smith, and Horace Greeley. It admits white and Black students of both sexes, welcomes all regardless of tongue or color, and offers knowledge without exclusive rights. In summer 1852 it has about ninety students, low fees, and work opportunities for poor students. Angeline Stickney enters as a junior in 1853, begins senior study in 1854, and remains intensely loyal to her Alma Mater.

takes_place_at New York Central College [for Angeline Stickney] ------------------------------------------------------------------------ CHAPTER V.] College attendance is Angeline Stickney's objective, and she is determined that Ruth will attend with her. McGrawville is selected because it permits both sisters to live together at very low cost, and Angeline eventually attends New York Central College.

l: Angeline Stickney's second journal, An Astronomer's Wife
s: Angeline Stickney’s second and last journal is a handmade stitched booklet with thin brown wrapping-paper covers. It follows her travel between towns, efforts to organize painting classes, expenses, teaching and discouragements, and progress through junior and senior years at New York Central College.

is_taught_by Angeline Stickney [as traveling instruction] ------------------------------------------------------------------------ CHAPTER V.] Monochromatic painting is one of the ways Angeline Stickney tries to raise money for college. She travels to places including Lockport, Felts Mills, Gouverneur, and Champion seeking pupils, sometimes forming small classes but often finding little interest.

l: New York Central College junior year, An Astronomer's Wife
s: is_a year of college study ------------------------------------------------------------------------ CHAPTER V.] Angeline Stickney enters the junior year at New York Central College in September 1853 after returning to McGrawville following about a year's absence. She considers the day of her entrance potentially one of the most important in her life.
